Subject : Reservoir Fluids Study, B21L Well
                Our Ref: MFL 20120023

Three (3) separator gas & three (3) separator liquid samples were collected from B21L well and forwarded to our Kuala Lumpur laboratory for reservoir fluid analysis. Presented in the following report are the results of all the analysis requested.

Core Laboratories Malaysia Sdn. Bhd. appreciates this opportunity to have been of service to PETRONAS Carigali Sdn Bhd. Manager
Reservoir Fluids Group

Sample Received
Three (3) separator liquid and three (3) separator gas samples collected from B21L well, were received in our Kuala Lumpur laboratory for reservoir fuid analyses. 

Surface Sample Validation (Separator Liquid)
The separator liquid samples were heated to a temperature of 200°F prior to any sample removal in order to eliminate any possible wax precipitation. Upon heating, the  water and mud  amounts in the sample were determined as a quality check. The samples were then transferred into Corelab cylinder prior further analysis and the original cylinders were returned to Halliburton.

Bubble Point Determination (Separator Liquid)
A portion of separator liquid  sample was charged to a high pressure visual PVT cell at reported separator temperature.  Saturation point determination was then performed during which the bubble point pressure was determined. 

Surface Sample Validation (Separator Gas)
The separator gas samples were agitated well and allowed to stabilized at respective separator temperature. The opening pressure, amount of mud and water and the hydrocarbon composition through dodecanes plus were then determined from the validation process. The samples were then transferred into Corelab cylinder prior further analysis and the original cylinders were returned to Halliburton. 

Sample Selection
Upon reviweing the Validation & Compositional Analysis Data, a representative of PETRONAS Carigali Sdn. Bhd has requested Corelab to perform physical recombination on sample from Cyl# 818735 (separator liquid) and Cyl# 2374 (separator gas) and adjustment of saturation pressure of the recombined reservoir fluid sample to 1100 psig at temperature 206°F. The recombined reservoir fluid sample was requested for further PVT analysis.

Sample Composition by Flash Separation
The composition of the selected separator liquid sample was determined using a flash separation technique and gas chromatography. The schematic diagram of flash separation technique is presented as Figure 1 on page A.4 of this report. The liquid was flashed at atmospheric pressure and a controlled temperature of 120°F and separated into gas and liquid phases.  The gas was analysed by extended gas analysis technique  and the liquid by temperature programmed  high resolution capillary gas chromatography. Refer Gas Composition and Stablised Liquid Composition (below) for detail explanation on gas chromatography techniques.  The two analyses were then mathematically recombined to the flash gas-liquid ratio. 

Gas Composition
Gas composition was determined using extended gas chromatography by the GPA 2286 method using a multi-column gas chromatograph system.  A single partial pressure charge is passed through the sampling valve and charged to each analytical column. The TCD (Thermal Conductivity Detector) reads O2, N2 and C1 from the molecular sieve column followed by C2, CO2, C3, iC4, nC4, iC5, nC5 from the porous polymer column. The FID (Flame Ionization Detector) reads up to Cn+ from the capillary column independently.   A temperature programme was used in order to provide optimum detection and resolution of the dodecanes plus components.

Stabilised Liquid Compositions
Stabilised liquid compositions were determined by temperature high resolution capillary gas chromatography using a cold-on-column injection technique. This injection technique involves the sample being deposited directly onto the front end of a wide bore capillary column. The sample is injected cold (35°C) to eliminate flashback through the injector port. Once the injection is complete, the front end of the column is rapidly heated to 300°C to vapourise the sample. The various constituents of the sample then elute through  the column at different retention times into a Flame Ionisation Detector (FID). The output or signal of the detector is proportional to the amount of a component or constituent present in the sample. Note that the FID response is proportional to the number of the carbon atoms, therefore the FID can be regarded as a mass detector.

Calculation of Mole%  Compositions and Plus Fraction Properties
The residue or stocktank liquid whole sample molecular weight and density are measured using a cryette and PAAR densitometer respectively.  A more detailed explanation of the operating principle of these instruments is described below.

The mole% data is calculated using GPSA mole weight and density data, where individual components are identified, from carbon dioxide through decanes. Katz and Firoozabadi data are used from undecanes through pentatriacontanes.  The residue mole weight and density values are calculated so that the pseudo average mole weight and density are the same as the measured values. This can lead to anomalous residue mole weights and densities where the Katz and Firoozabadi values may not be suitable for the isomer groups detected.

Other alternatives are to use an assumed C36+ molecular weight and density value, use a linear extrapolation technique for components from C10 to C35 to calculate the C36+ properties or to utilise distillation analysis to produce a C12+, C20+ or C36+ residual oil fraction and physically measure the molecular weight and density.

Molecular Weight (whole sample Molecular Weight measurement by Cryoscope)
The cryoscope works on principle of the freezing point depression technique (Cryoscopy) for molecular weight measurement. Freezing-point depression is the difference between the freezing points of a pure solvent and a solution of a non-electrolyte in that solvent.
Since the freezing point of a pure solvent (such as benzene) is lowered when a solute (oil) is added, a precise temperature-measuring system is calibrated using pure hydrocarbons of known molecular weight.  The observed depression of the freezing point temperature (Delta T) is then used to calculate the molecular weight of solute (oil) sample. The cryoscope is calibrated daily using n-nonane, n-pentadecane and squalane.  Directly following the calibration the cryoscope is checked with n-C14 (n-tetradecane) which has a known molecular weight of 198.40 g mole-1.  If the molecular weight value determined using the cryoscope falls outside an acceptable error band, the calibration is then repeated.
Before using the whole sample molecular weight to balance the measured composition the molecular weight is corrected to account for the naturally occurring benzene present in the sample. The naturally occuring benzene is determined by the gas chromatography.

Density (whole sample density measurement)
Measurement of the density for oil, hydrocarbon fractions and residues are performed using a Paar Densitometer using IP methodologies.  The Paar Densitometer measures density via the determination a change in oscillation frequency for a vibrating glass U-tube.  The system is first calibrated by filling the tube with known density standards (air and distilled water).  It is then filled with the oil to be measured. A calibration function is used to relate the oscillation frequencies to density.  Each sample is run in duplicate and the results must agree within 0.001 g cm-3.

FULL BLACK OIL STUDY 

Constant Composition Expansion
A Constant Composition Expansion (CCE) was carried out at reservoir temperature during which the bubble point pressure was determined.  Pressure-volume data for the single phase and two phase fluid were also determined at the reservoir temperature.  The density of the single phase fluid was determined by weighing measured volumes pumped from the cell at 5000 psig.  Density data for other pressures were calculated using the volumetric data. 

Differential Vaporisation
Differential Vaporisation was carried out in a high pressure visual cell, at reservoir temperature. The sample was agitated below the observed saturation pressure and allowed to stabilise at several stages.  The gas evolved was then pumped out of the cell during which the volume and compressibility were also determined.  The final stage was carried out at atmospheric pressure by pumping out the residual liquid from the cell and its properties (density and mole weight) were also measured. 

Viscosity
The viscosity of reservoir fluid bottomhole oil sample was measured in a Electromagnetic  Viscometer (EMV) at reservoir temperature.  Viscosity determinations were carried out over a wide range of pressures from above the reservoir pressure to atmospheric pressure.

EMV piston-style viscometer contains two magnetic coils inside a stainless steel body. A low mass stainless steel piston inside the measurement chamber is magnetically forced back and forth in the fluid. The time required for the piston to move a fixed distance (about  0.2 inches) is then very accurately related to the viscosity of the fluid in the chamber by use of calibration constants. The viscosity measurements were repeated at each pressure stage until five or more results agreed to within 0.5% of each other.  

Separator Tests
One multi stage separator test at condition (144 psig @ 115°F, 41 psig @ 138°F, 5 psig @ 135°F & 0 psig @ 60°F) was performed by using a pressurised separator test cell.  A portion of the recombined reservoir fluid sample was pumped into the separator cell at a pressure above the saturation pressure, followed by stabilising sample at the pressure and temperature required.  The gas evolved was pumped out of the cell and the volume and composition were determined.  The final stage was carried out at atmospheric pressure  and the density of the residual liquid was determined.

Physical Recombination
A portion of the selected separator gas and separator liquid sample were physically recombined to obtain a recombined reservoir fluid sample having saturation pressure of 1100 psig at 206°F.The recombined reservoir fluid sample (Cyl# TS 100002) was then subjected to compositional analysis prior further PVT study.

Recombined Reservoir Fluid Sample Composition by Flash Separation
The composition of the recombined reservoir fluid sample were determined using a flash separation technique and gas chromatography. The sample was flashed at atmospheric pressure and a controlled temperature of 120°F and separated into gas and liquid phases.  The gas was analysed by extended gas analysis technique  and the liquid by temperature programmed high resolution capillary gas chromatography. The two analyses were then mathematically recombined to the flash gas-liquid ratio.
